## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview, vv. 28–53 (Ligonier, Reformed):** David was weak but still had his wits. Once Nathan and Bathsheba told him what was happening, David took action. Ligonier's application is that David's men didn't wait for a miraculous sign. Believers should act wisely by Scripture and not wait for a "sign from heaven," nor are we to "let go and let God." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomon-anointed-king

**v. 29:** Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) calls David's oath, made at the end of his life, David's glorious witness. And this is the end of his life, the end of the road. What a beautiful witness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-51.html

**v. 33 (the mule):**
- Riding the king's own mule showed that royal power was being handed over with David's consent (Benson, Poole). Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary pass on a rabbinic tradition that riding the king's mule without permission was punishable by death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-33.htm
- Clarke (Methodist) says no subject could use anything belonging to the king without losing his life, so the mule was full evidence that he had appointed him his successor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-33.html
- Pulpit notes that mules seem to have been a recent import, and Israelites were forbidden to breed them. That is why their use was limited to royalty and important people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-33.htm

**v. 33 (Gihon):**
- The commentators disagree about where Gihon was. Poole and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown put it west of Jerusalem. Poole sets it against En-rogel, where Adonijah was feasting, on the east side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-33.htm
- Ellicott thinks a site south of the city is more likely. One commentary on the same page says Gihon was not a holy place - but purely as a demonstration to the populace, and to checkmate the conspirators. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/1-33.htm
- The Aramaic Targum reads "Siloam." Kimchi says David chose the spring as a good omen: as its waters never fail, so might Solomon's kingdom last. https://biblehub.com/study/1_kings/1-33.htm
- The Gospel Coalition commentary (Konkel) describes Gihon as the source of water for Jerusalem in the Kidron valley next to the city of David. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-kings/

**v. 39 (the oil):**
- Most commentators say this was the holy anointing oil of Exodus 30. Clarke adds that horns were commonly used as containers, and that this oil anointed both priests and kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-39.html
- Which "tent" was it? Keil & Delitzsch and Barnes say David's tent for the ark on Mount Zion, not the tabernacle at Gibeon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-39.htm
- Ellicott agrees the oil came from the Zion tent because of the hurry, but notes the main tabernacle was at Gibeon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-39.htm
- A Bible Hub Q&A article says instead that the tent was the tabernacle at Gibeon. https://biblehub.com/q/Horn_of_oil_s_role_in_1_Kings_1_39.htm
- Konkel (Gospel Coalition) says the oil from the ark's tent shows the anointing was divinely commissioned, not merely the desire of the king and his supporters. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-kings/
- Gill reports a Jewish view that a king's son didn't normally need anointing. Solomon was anointed because of Adonijah's revolt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-39.htm
- Matthew Henry contrasts the two claimants: Adonijah was made king by a feast, not by an unction. He also sees the anointing as a picture of Christ, on whom the Spirit was poured without measure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-39.html
- Pulpit points out that the three parts of David's order in v. 34 were carried out exactly. Solomon was confirmed by the people's acclaim. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/1-39.htm

**v. 40:** Ligonier says the public anointing brought great acclaim, and so much joy that the earth split. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomon-anointed-king

**vv. 43–48 (Jonathan's report):** The Cambridge Bible notes that Jonathan keeps repeating "and also." That piles up details exactly after the style of a messenger in great haste. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-48.htm

**v. 46:** Constable says Solomon now sat on the throne as David's co-regent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-39.html

**v. 47:**
- The Cambridge Bible notes that a son beginning to reign while his father was still alive was common in the East. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-47.htm
- The word for "bowed" is the usual word for worship. Keil compares David to Jacob worshipping on his bed (Genesis 47:31). Pulpit suggests Jonathan may be crediting the servants with Benaiah's words from vv. 36–37. Same page.

**v. 48:**
- Barnes says David worshipped and prayed that the blessing would come true, and points to Hebrews 11:21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-48.htm
- Gill says David credits the whole affair to God's providence, even though it happened on his own orders. Same page.
- The Cambridge Bible says David was thankful for this particular son, not just for any successor. Same page.
- Pulpit notes that it was very unusual for a king to see his successor on the throne. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/1-48.htm

**v. 49:** Keil: The news spread terror. All the guests of Adonijah fled, every man his way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-50.htm

**v. 50 (horns of the altar):**
- Ellicott says the Law didn't give sanctuary to deliberate murderers (Exodus 21:14). Adonijah seems to present his grab for power as a hasty, unintended act, the only kind sanctuary covered. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/1-50.htm
- Benson says sanctuary at the altar came from custom among the nations, not from the Law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-50.htm
- Keil, quoting Bähr, says grasping the horns put the guilty man under the protection of God's saving grace. Same page.
- JFB calls the horns symbols of grace and salvation to the sinner. Same page.
- Which altar? Pulpit and Keil think Zion is most likely but say it can't be known for sure. Gill prefers the altar on Araunah's threshing floor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-50.htm
- Matthew Henry warns that people who neglect salvation while they feel safe may when it is too late, will catch hold of the horns of the altar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-50.html

**v. 52:**
- Barnes calls Solomon's mercy very remarkable. In the East not only are pretenders almost always punished with death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/1-52.html
- Poole says the Hebrew phrase means "a man of strength." He sees both kindness and good sense in Solomon sparing his older brother. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-52.htm
- Enduring Word says the pardon went against all custom in the ancient world. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-1/
- Enduring Word later treats Adonijah's execution in chapter 2 as Solomon acting on these "terms of parole". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-2/

**v. 53:**
- By bowing, Adonijah recognised Solomon as his king. "Go to your house" meant living a quiet, private life away from public affairs (Benson). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-52.htm
- Keil says the words gave Adonijah his life and his freedom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/1-53.htm

## Differences between traditions
I didn't find any real denominational split on these verses. Commentators from different traditions disagree on details, not doctrine: where Gihon was, which tent the oil came from, which altar Adonijah grabbed. Those are listed above. Older Reformed, Methodist, Anglican and Calvary Chapel writers (Henry, JFB, Clarke, Ellicott, Smith) all read the scene as God installing his chosen king.

## Modern scholarship
**v. 52:** The NET Bible translates the condition as being a "loyal subject" versus being found "to be a traitor", which reads it in political terms. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=1Ki&chapter=1&verse=52
